title: Reliable Control-Point Selection for Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models

paper.title: Reliable Control-Point Selection for Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Steering vectors offer a training-free mechanism for controlling reasoning behaviors in large language models, but constructing effective vectors requires identifying genuine behavioral signals in the model’s hidden states. For behaviors that can be toggled via prompts, this is straightforward. However, many reasoning behaviors—such as self-reflection—emerge spontaneously and resist prompt-level control. Current methods detect these behaviors through keyword matching in chain-of-thought traces, implicitly assuming that every detected boundary encodes a genuine behavioral signal. We show that this assumption is overwhelmingly wrong: across 541 keyword-detected boundaries, 93.3% are behaviorally unstable, failing to reproduce the detected behavior under re-generation from the same prefix. We develop a probabilistic model that formalizes intrinsic reasoning behaviors as stochastic events with context-dependent trigger probabilities, and show that unstable boundaries dilute the steering signal. Guided by this analysis, we propose stability filtering, which retains only boundaries where the model consistently reproduces the target behavior. Combined with a content-subspace projection that removes residual question-specific noise, our method achieves 0.784 accuracy on MATH-500 (+5.0 over the strongest baseline). The resulting steering vectors transfer across models in the same architecture family without re-extraction, improving Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-1.5B (+5.0) and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview (+6.0). Code is available at https://github.com/zhmzm/stability-steering .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent large language models solve complex tasks by generating extended chains of thought before producing a final answer ( Wei et al., 2023 ) . During this reasoning process, models spontaneously exhibit distinct behavioral patterns—reflecting on intermediate results, switching strategies when stuck, verifying conclusions before committing ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . These behaviors often improve accuracy, but they can also be counterproductive: models frequently over-reflect or repeat unproductive steps, wasting tokens without improving solutions ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Sui et al., 2025 ) . Steering vectors offer a training-free mechanism for controlling such behaviors by adding learned directions to hidden states during generation ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) . The standard approach constructs a steering direction by contrasting hidden states with and without the target behavior, then applies this direction at inference time. Constructing effective steering vectors in such manners requires identifying where genuine behavioral signals are encoded. For behaviors that can be toggled via prompts—such as output format or response style—this is straightforward: one contrasts hidden states with and without the target instruction. However, many reasoning behaviors resist prompt-level control. A model may pause to verify an intermediate result, yet instructing it to “reflect less” neither suppresses the pattern nor yields a useful steering direction (§ 4.2 ). For such behaviors, one must instead extract signals from the model’s own reasoning traces, typically by detecting behavioral boundaries through surface-level cues such as keyword matching ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . This raises a fundamental question: does a detected boundary actually reflect a genuine behavioral commitment by the model? We find that, overwhelmingly, it does not. The core issue is that intrinsic reasoning behaviors are stochastic: at any given position, a model may or may not produce the target behavior across independent generations. A keyword match at such a position is therefore a noisy proxy—it may capture a genuine behavioral commitment or a coincidental surface pattern. Through systematic re-generation experiments across 541 keyword-detected boundaries, we find that 93.3% are behaviorally unstable: the detected behavior fails to reproduce when the model is re-run from the same prefix. The mean trigger probability is only p ¯ = 0.167 \bar{p}=0.167 , indicating that existing methods retain roughly one-sixth of the maximum possible behavioral signal. Figure 1 : Extrinsic behaviors are steered via prompt contrast (left). Intrinsic behaviors emerge spontaneously and resist prompting (middle-left). Keyword matching detects them from traces (middle-right), but most detections are unstable under re-generation (right; data from § 4.3 ). This observation motivates a simple principle: only behaviorally stable boundaries should contribute to the steering vector . We estimate each boundary’s trigger probability by re-generating from its prefix multiple times, then retain only those that consistently reproduce the target behavior. A probabilistic analysis shows that this filtering amplifies the behavioral signal in proportion to the ratio of filtered to unfiltered trigger probabilities, and predicts that hard thresholding should outperform soft weighting when the trigger distribution is skewed—both predictions are confirmed experimentally. Combined with a content-subspace projection that removes residual question-specific noise, our method yields substantial improvements over the strongest existing baseline on MATH-500, and the resulting steering vectors can be transferred across models within the same architecture family without re-extraction . Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We develop a probabilistic model of intrinsic reasoning behaviors that formalizes them as stochastic events with context-dependent trigger probabilities, explains why surface-detected boundaries dilute the steering signal, and yields testable predictions about filtering strategies. 2. We propose stability filtering , a method that estimates trigger probabilities via repeated sampling and retains only high-probability boundaries. Combined with content-subspace projection, this achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on MATH-500 across three models. A behavior probe confirms that stable boundaries carry stronger behavioral signals in their hidden states. 3. We demonstrate cross-model transfer : steering vectors extracted once from a single source model improve two additional models in the same architecture family, without any model-specific re-extraction.

sections.heading: Reasoning in LLMs.
sections.text: Chain-of-thought prompting ( Wei et al., 2023 ) established that LLMs can solve complex reasoning tasks by generating intermediate steps, and subsequent work has extended this through self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , tree-of-thought search ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , step-level verification ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , and self-reflection ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Reinforcement learning has further amplified these capabilities: DeepSeek-R1 ( Guo et al., 2025 ) uses RL without supervised fine-tuning to induce self-verification and extended chain-of-thought, achieving strong performance on math and code benchmarks. Test-time compute scaling ( Zeng et al., 2025 ) shows that allocating more inference tokens improves reasoning, but this comes at a cost. Recent work has identified an overthinking problem ( Sui et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) : models frequently over-reflect or repeat unproductive reasoning steps, wasting tokens without improving accuracy. Controlling these intrinsic reasoning behaviors is the central motivation of our work.

sections.heading: Steering vectors for LLMs.
sections.text: Controllable generation in LLMs has been explored through both training-time and inference-time interventions ( Dathathri et al., 2020 ) . Activation steering ( Turner et al., 2024 ) showed that adding fixed directions to residual stream activations can induce behavioral changes, and subsequent work has applied this principle to truthfulness ( Li et al., 2024 ) , safety and refusal ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , personality traits ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and contrastive behavior control ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Zou et al. (2025) proposed representation engineering as a general framework for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in LLMs. The theoretical basis for these methods rests on the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ; Burns et al., 2024 ) , which posits that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in residual stream space. For reasoning specifically, SEAL ( Chen et al., 2025b ) introduced a lightweight approach to calibrating reasoning behaviors via hidden-state contrasts extracted from chain-of-thought traces, and Sinii et al. (2026) provided a mechanistic analysis of how steering vectors modify reasoning. Venhoff et al. (2025) systematically mapped steering directions to distinct reasoning behaviors. Our work builds directly on SEAL’s pipeline but addresses a fundamental limitation: the assumption that keyword-detected boundaries all encode genuine behavioral signals.

sections.heading: Stochastic behaviors and robustness.
sections.text: Our work is grounded in the observation that intrinsic reasoning behaviors are stochastic rather than deterministic. Dies et al. (2026) showed that LLM belief representations can be unstable under semantic perturbations, and Wang et al. (2022) noted that behavioral features in language models vary across sampling conditions. Perez et al. (2022) demonstrated that model-written evaluations can reveal inconsistent behaviors that are not apparent from single-sample analysis. Our stability probing methodology is related to consistency-based filtering in data curation ( Swayamdipta et al., 2020 ) , where training examples are classified by their learning dynamics. We apply an analogous principle to steering vector construction: only boundaries where the model stochastically reproduces the target behavior with high probability should contribute to the steering direction.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Figure 2 : Overview of our method. Left : SEAL mixes all keyword-detected boundaries, including unstable ones that dilute the signal. Middle : Our content-aware extraction computes per-question steering directions and projects out question-specific information via SVD. Right : Stability probing re-generates from each boundary’s prefix and retains only those that reliably reproduce the target behavior. Figure 2 gives an overview of our approach. We start from the SEAL pipeline (§ 3.1 ), identify why it underperforms through a probabilistic lens (§ 3.2 ), and propose two fixes: stability filtering (§ 3.3 ) and content projection (§ 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries: SEAL Steering Vectors
sections.text: Given a reasoning LLM and a problem set 𝒬 = { q 1 , … , q N } \mathcal{Q}=\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}\} , SEAL ( Chen et al., 2025b ) constructs a steering vector as follows. For each problem q k q_{k} , the model generates a chain-of-thought response, which is segmented into paragraphs. Each paragraph is classified as a behavior boundary or an execution segment based on the presence of reasoning-related keywords (e.g., “wait,” “verify,” “alternatively”), yielding boundary positions B k B_{k} and execution positions E k E_{k} . All hidden states below are extracted at the first token of each paragraph at a target layer ℓ \ell ; we write 𝐡 b ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{h}_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and suppress the layer index for clarity. A per-example steering vector is computed as: 𝐝 k = 1 | B k | ​ ∑ b ∈ B k 𝐡 b − 1 | E k | ​ ∑ e ∈ E k 𝐡 e , \mathbf{d}_{k}=\frac{1}{|B_{k}|}\sum_{b\in B_{k}}\mathbf{h}_{b}-\frac{1}{|E_{k}|}\sum_{e\in E_{k}}\mathbf{h}_{e}, (1) where the first term averages over behavior boundary hidden states and the second over execution hidden states. The final SEAL vector is 𝐯 seal = normalize ​ ( 1 N ​ ∑ k 𝐝 k ) \mathbf{v}_{\text{seal}}=\text{normalize}(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\mathbf{d}_{k}) . Problems where | B k | = 0 |B_{k}|=0 or | E k | = 0 |E_{k}|=0 are excluded. At inference, the steering vector is applied at paragraph boundaries within the <think> block: 𝐡 ← 𝐡 + α ⋅ 𝐯 seal \mathbf{h}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}+\alpha\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\text{seal}} , using the same keyword rules for boundary detection.

sections.heading: 3.2 Why SEAL’s Signal Is Diluted
sections.text: The core issue with SEAL is that keyword matching is a poor proxy for genuine behavior. A paragraph containing “wait” may or may not reflect an actual reflective reasoning step. We formalize this with a simple probabilistic model. The analysis below uses idealizing assumptions and is meant as motivation, not as a formal guarantee, we test its predictions experimentally in § 4.3 – 4.4 .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: Recall from §1 that intrinsic behaviors emerge spontaneously during reasoning and cannot be reliably controlled through prompts. At each candidate boundary b b with context c b c_{b} , we define a trigger probability p b = P ⁡ ( behavior ​ a ∣ c b ) p_{b}=P(\text{behavior }a\mid c_{b}) , where a a is the event that the model produces a genuine behavior boundary. Following SEAL, we merge Reflection (R) and Transition (T) into one class and treat the problem as binary. Since p b p_{b} is not directly observable, keyword detection is a noisy proxy; our stability probing (§ 3.3 ) estimates p b p_{b} empirically. We model the hidden state at boundary b b with a latent commitment indicator z b ∼ Bernoulli ​ ( p b ) z_{b}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p_{b}) : 𝐡 b = z b ⋅ 𝜹 + 𝝁 ⁡ ( c b ) + ϵ b , \mathbf{h}_{b}=z_{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{\delta}+\boldsymbol{\mu}(c_{b})+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{b}, (2) where 𝜹 ∈ ℝ D \boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is a shared behavioral direction, 𝝁 ⁡ ( c b ) \boldsymbol{\mu}(c_{b}) is context-dependent (question content, reasoning state), and ϵ b \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{b} is residual noise. sections.heading: 3.4 Content-Subspace Projection
sections.text: A separate source of noise in the steering vector is question-specific content. The SEAL per-example vector (Eq. 1 ) subtracts the execution mean from the boundary mean, but the two groups are not aligned: they differ in size ( | B k | ≠ | E k | |B_{k}|\neq|E_{k}| ) and occupy systematically different positions in the reasoning chain. Boundaries tend to appear at harder or more uncertain junctures, while execution segments dominate routine computation. As a result, the subtraction does not fully cancel the context term 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} , and the residual carries question-level information such as math subject or problem difficulty. To remove this, we estimate the “question-specific directions” from question-only hidden states and project them out. This is a heuristic: we do not know that the residual in 𝐝 k \mathbf{d}_{k} falls exactly in this subspace, but question-only representations provide a reasonable proxy for the directions we want to suppress. Concretely, for each problem k k we feed only the question text through the model and mean-pool hidden states at layer ℓ \ell to get 𝐪 k ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{q}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . We center the matrix 𝐐 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} and take its SVD: 𝐐 c = 𝐔 ​ 𝚺 ​ 𝐕 ⊤ \mathbf{Q}_{c}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} . The top- K K right singular vectors 𝐕 K ∈ ℝ D × K \mathbf{V}_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times K} define the content subspace. We assume that 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} has negligible projection onto this subspace. This is an approximation: if 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} does overlap, projection will attenuate the signal. The rank K K controls the trade-off; we use K = 4 K{=}4 based on probing results (§ 4.5 ). Each steering vector is projected out: 𝐝 k ⟂ = 𝐝 k − 𝐕 K ​ ( 𝐕 K ⊤ ​ 𝐝 k ) , \mathbf{d}_{k}^{\perp}=\mathbf{d}_{k}-\mathbf{V}_{K}(\mathbf{V}_{K}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{k}), (7) and the projected vector is 𝐯 proj = normalize ​ ( 1 N ​ ∑ k 𝐝 k ⟂ ) \mathbf{v}_{\text{proj}}=\text{normalize}(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\mathbf{d}_{k}^{\perp}) . By linearity, this is equivalent to projecting each 𝐡 b \mathbf{h}_{b} and 𝐡 e \mathbf{h}_{e} individually before computing the difference.

sections.text: The final steering vector combines both fixes. We first filter for stable boundaries, then project out the content subspace: 𝐯 A+B = normalize ​ ( 1 N ′ ​ ∑ k [ 1 | B k τ | ​ ∑ b ∈ B k τ 𝐡 b ⟂ − 1 | E k | ​ ∑ e ∈ E k 𝐡 e ⟂ ] ) , \mathbf{v}_{\text{A+B}}=\text{normalize}\!\left(\frac{1}{N^{\prime}}\sum_{k}\left[\frac{1}{|B_{k}^{\tau}|}\sum_{b\in B_{k}^{\tau}}\mathbf{h}_{b}^{\perp}-\frac{1}{|E_{k}|}\sum_{e\in E_{k}}\mathbf{h}_{e}^{\perp}\right]\right), (8) where 𝐡 ⟂ = 𝐡 − 𝐕 K ​ ( 𝐕 K ⊤ ​ 𝐡 ) \mathbf{h}^{\perp}=\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{V}_{K}(\mathbf{V}_{K}^{\top}\mathbf{h}) and B k τ = { b ∈ B k : s ⁡ ( b ) ≥ τ } B_{k}^{\tau}=\{b\in B_{k}:s(b)\geq\tau\} . Filtering improves the signal (better alignment with 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} ); projection aims to reduce residual content noise. We ablate their individual and combined contributions in § 4.2 .

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We extract steering vectors from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and evaluate on the same model. To test cross-model transfer, we apply the same vectors (without re-extraction) to two additional Qwen-architecture 1.5B models: Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-1.5B and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview. All models produce chain-of-thought reasoning within <think> blocks.

sections.heading: Data and evaluation protocol.
sections.text: Steering vectors are extracted from 100 MATH training problems and evaluated on MATH-500 (test set, 500 questions). All main results (Table 1 ) use max_tokens=4096 with greedy decoding (temperature 0). Accuracy is measured by exact match against the ground-truth answer after extracting the final \boxed{} expression.

sections.heading: Hyperparameters.
sections.text: Steering is applied at layer 20, corresponding to 71% depth in the 28-layer Qwen architecture. The steering coefficient α = − 100 \alpha{=}-100 is selected on a held-out set. The stability threshold τ = 0.8 \tau{=}0.8 is selected from a sweep at max_tokens=1024 (§ 4.4 ) and then held fixed for the main 4096-token evaluation; the content-subspace rank K = 4 K{=}4 is chosen based on the probing analysis in § 4.5 . Full coefficient sweeps for all methods are reported in Appendix A and B .

sections.heading: Prompt baselines.
sections.text: To ground the intrinsic/extrinsic distinction from §1, we include two prompt-based interventions in the same table. Adding “use less reflection” to the prompt yields 0.672 (+6.4), and a prompt-derived steering vector ( 𝐡 Q + prompt − 𝐡 Q \mathbf{h}_{Q+\text{prompt}}-\mathbf{h}_{Q} ) achieves only 0.610 (+0.2). Both fall well below activation steering (0.784). While we tested only a limited set of prompt formulations, these results are consistent with reflection being an intrinsic behavior that resists prompt-level control.

sections.heading: Cross-model transfer.
sections.text: The same steering vectors, extracted once from Qwen-1.5B, also work on other Qwen-architecture 1.5B models without re-extraction. On Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-1.5B, our method achieves 0.816 (+15.4 over baseline) vs. SEAL’s 0.766. On DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview, our method achieves 0.812 (+8.6) vs. SEAL’s 0.752. These models share the same architecture and were trained on similar reasoning data, which likely explains why the steering direction transfers. Whether this extends to more distant model families remains an open question.

sections.heading: 4.3 How Unstable Are Keyword-Detected Boundaries?

(b) Accuracy peaks at τ = 0.8 \tau{=}0.8 (+7.0 over SEAL), then drops at τ = 0.9 \tau{=}0.9 as sample size shrinks. Shaded band shows random baseline ± 1 ​ σ \pm 1\sigma . If the stochastic model in § 3.2 is roughly right, we should expect two things: (i) most keyword-detected boundaries have low trigger probability p b p_{b} , and (ii) the distribution of p b p_{b} should be heavily skewed rather than smoothly spread. Both predictions are borne out by Figure 3 (a). Across 541 keyword-detected behavior boundaries (Reflection and Transition) extracted from 100 problems, 292 (54%) have s ⁡ ( b ) = 0 s(b)=0 : the behavior never reappears across 10 independent re-generations from the same prefix. Only 36 (6.7%) meet or exceed τ = 0.8 \tau{=}0.8 . The distribution is heavily zero-inflated with a long right tail: beyond the spike at zero, scores decay gradually through the 0.1–0.7 range before a small cluster at s ≥ 0.8 s\geq 0.8 . This is consistent with keyword matching picking up a large population of coincidental matches ( p b ≈ 0 p_{b}\approx 0 ) alongside a small minority of genuine behavioral commitments. The mean trigger probability is p ¯ = 0.167 \bar{p}=0.167 . Substituting into our dilution analysis (Eq. 3 ), this implies the SEAL vector retains roughly 17% of the maximum behavioral signal. The heavy concentration of mass near zero also explains why hard thresholding (+7.0 over SEAL) substantially outperforms soft weighting (+2.2): low- p b p_{b} boundaries dominate the average under any continuous weighting scheme, and only a hard cutoff can exclude them entirely.

sections.heading: 4.4 Does Filtering Actually Help?
sections.text: The theory predicts that filtering for high- p b p_{b} boundaries should amplify the steering signal. We test this with a threshold sweep, then check two potential confounds.

sections.heading: Threshold sweep.
sections.text: Figure 3 (b) shows accuracy as a function of τ \tau , evaluated at max_tokens=1024 on MATH-500. We use a shorter token budget here for computational efficiency; the main results in Table 1 use 4096. The stability-filtered vector (0.496) lies 3.1 ​ σ 3.1\sigma above this baseline, so the gain comes from boundary quality, not quantity. sections.heading: Why does filtering help? A probing analysis.
sections.text: The accuracy gains above are consistent with our theory, but do stable boundaries actually carry a stronger behavioral signal in their hidden states? We train a balanced logistic regression probe to classify hidden states at layer 20 as behavior boundary vs. execution (methodology details in Appendix C ). Figure 4 shows that the most stable boundaries ( s ≥ 0.8 s\geq 0.8 ) achieve a probe confidence of 0.942 , while the least stable ( s < 0.2 s<0.2 ) score only 0.721 (overall accuracy 0.818, ρ = + 0.165 \rho={+}0.165 ). This is what we expect from Eq. 2 : higher p b p_{b} means more 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} in the hidden state, which the probe picks up as a stronger boundary signal.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that the majority of reasoning boundaries identified by keyword matching in LLM chain-of-thought traces are behaviorally unstable. 93.3% fail to consistently reproduce the target reasoning behavior across re-generations. By filtering for behavioral stability and projecting out question-specific content, we construct steering vectors that achieve 0.784 accuracy on MATH-500, a 5% improvement over SEAL. These vectors transfer effectively across models within the same architecture family, improving Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-1.5B by 5% and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview by 6% over their respective SEAL baselines. A balanced behavior probe confirms that stable boundaries encode cleaner behavioral signals in hidden states.

sections.heading: Behavior probe (R+T vs. E).
sections.text: We train a logistic regression classifier ( LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=1.0, solver=‘lbfgs’) ) to distinguish behavior boundary (R+T) hidden states from execution (E) hidden states at layer 20. We partition the 541 R+T boundaries into 5 equal stability bins of width 0.2 on [ 0 , 1 ) [0,1) and sample 22 boundaries per bin, yielding 110 R+T samples total. We then downsample E to 110 samples, giving a balanced dataset of 220 total samples spanning 88 unique questions. Cross-validation uses GroupKFold ( n = 5 n{=}5 folds) grouped by question_id to prevent data leakage across folds.

sections.heading: SVD content subspace probe.
sections.text: We probe 100 question hidden states (one per extraction question) decomposed under varying truncation ranks k k . The 100 questions span 7 MATH subjects; we use StratifiedKFold ( n = 5 n{=}5 ) by subject label. For each k k , we train separate probes on the rank- k k projection Q ∥ Q_{\parallel} and the orthogonal residual Q ⟂ Q_{\perp} , measuring 7-class subject classification accuracy.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2604.02113v1 [cs.CL] 02 Apr 2026 Reliable Control-Point Selection for Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models Haomin Zhuang, Hojun Yoo, Xiaonan Luo, Kehan Guo, Xiangliang Zhang University of Notre Dame {hzhuang2, xzhang33}@nd.edu Abstract Steering vectors offer a training-free mechanism for controlling reasoning behaviors in large language models, but constructing effective vectors requires identifying genuine behavioral signals in the model’s hidden states. For behaviors that can be toggled via prompts, this is straightforward. However, many reasoning behaviors—such as self-reflection—emerge spontaneously and resist prompt-level control. Current methods detect these behaviors through keyword matching in chain-of-thought traces, implicitly assuming that every detected boundary encodes a genuine behavioral signal. We show that this assumption is overwhelmingly wrong: across 541 keyword-detected boundaries, 93.3% are behaviorally unstable, failing to reproduce the detected behavior under re-generation from the same prefix. We develop a probabilistic model that formalizes intrinsic reasoning behaviors as stochastic events with context-dependent trigger probabilities, and show that unstable boundaries dilute the steering signal. Guided by this analysis, we propose stability filtering, which retains only boundaries where the model consistently reproduces the target behavior. Combined with a content-subspace projection that removes residual question-specific noise, our method achieves 0.784 accuracy on MATH-500 (+5.0 over the strongest baseline). The resulting steering vectors transfer across models in the same architecture family without re-extraction, improving Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-1.5B (+5.0) and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview (+6.0). Code is available at https://github.com/zhmzm/stability-steering . 1 Introduction Recent large language models solve complex tasks by generating extended chains of thought before producing a final answer ( Wei et al., 2023 ) . During this reasoning process, models spontaneously exhibit distinct behavioral patterns—reflecting on intermediate results, switching strategies when stuck, verifying conclusions before committing ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . These behaviors often improve accuracy, but they can also be counterproductive: models frequently over-reflect or repeat unproductive steps, wasting tokens without improving solutions ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Sui et al., 2025 ) . Steering vectors offer a training-free mechanism for controlling such behaviors by adding learned directions to hidden states during generation ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) . The standard approach constructs a steering direction by contrasting hidden states with and without the target behavior, then applies this direction at inference time. Constructing effective steering vectors in such manners requires identifying where genuine behavioral signals are encoded. For behaviors that can be toggled via prompts—such as output format or response style—this is straightforward: one contrasts hidden states with and without the target instruction. However, many reasoning behaviors resist prompt-level control. A model may pause to verify an intermediate result, yet instructing it to “reflect less” neither suppresses the pattern nor yields a useful steering direction (§ 4.2 ). For such behaviors, one must instead extract signals from the model’s own reasoning traces, typically by detecting behavioral boundaries through surface-level cues such as keyword matching ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . This raises a fundamental question: does a detected boundary actually reflect a genuine behavioral commitment by the model? We find that, overwhelmingly, it does not. The core issue is that intrinsic reasoning behaviors are stochastic: at any given position, a model may or may not produce the target behavior across independent generations. A keyword match at such a position is therefore a noisy proxy—it may capture a genuine behavioral commitment or a coincidental surface pattern. Through systematic re-generation experiments across 541 keyword-detected boundaries, we find that 93.3% are behaviorally unstable: the detected behavior fails to reproduce when the model is re-run from the same prefix. The mean trigger probability is only p ¯ = 0.167 \bar{p}=0.167 , indicating that existing methods retain roughly one-sixth of the maximum possible behavioral signal. Figure 1 : Extrinsic behaviors are steered via prompt contrast (left). Intrinsic behaviors emerge spontaneously and resist prompting (middle-left). Keyword matching detects them from traces (middle-right), but most detections are unstable under re-generation (right; data from § 4.3 ). This observation motivates a simple principle: only behaviorally stable boundaries should contribute to the steering vector . We estimate each boundary’s trigger probability by re-generating from its prefix multiple times, then retain only those that consistently reproduce the target behavior. A probabilistic analysis shows that this filtering amplifies the behavioral signal in proportion to the ratio of filtered to unfiltered trigger probabilities, and predicts that hard thresholding should outperform soft weighting when the trigger distribution is skewed—both predictions are confirmed experimentally. Combined with a content-subspace projection that removes residual question-specific noise, our method yields substantial improvements over the strongest existing baseline on MATH-500, and the resulting steering vectors can be transferred across models within the same architecture family without re-extraction . Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We develop a probabilistic model of intrinsic reasoning behaviors that formalizes them as stochastic events with context-dependent trigger probabilities, explains why surface-detected boundaries dilute the steering signal, and yields testable predictions about filtering strategies. 2. We propose stability filtering , a method that estimates trigger probabilities via repeated sampling and retains only high-probability boundaries. Combined with content-subspace projection, this achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on MATH-500 across three models. A behavior probe confirms that stable boundaries carry stronger behavioral signals in their hidden states. 3. We demonstrate cross-model transfer : steering vectors extracted once from a single source model improve two additional models in the same architecture family, without any model-specific re-extraction. 2 Related Work Reasoning in LLMs. Chain-of-thought prompting ( Wei et al., 2023 ) established that LLMs can solve complex reasoning tasks by generating intermediate steps, and subsequent work has extended this through self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , tree-of-thought search ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , step-level verification ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , and self-reflection ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Reinforcement learning has further amplified these capabilities: DeepSeek-R1 ( Guo et al., 2025 ) uses RL without supervised fine-tuning to induce self-verification and extended chain-of-thought, achieving strong performance on math and code benchmarks. Test-time compute scaling ( Zeng et al., 2025 ) shows that allocating more inference tokens improves reasoning, but this comes at a cost. Recent work has identified an overthinking problem ( Sui et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) : models frequently over-reflect or repeat unproductive reasoning steps, wasting tokens without improving accuracy. Controlling these intrinsic reasoning behaviors is the central motivation of our work. Steering vectors for LLMs. Controllable generation in LLMs has been explored through both training-time and inference-time interventions ( Dathathri et al., 2020 ) . Activation steering ( Turner et al., 2024 ) showed that adding fixed directions to residual stream activations can induce behavioral changes, and subsequent work has applied this principle to truthfulness ( Li et al., 2024 ) , safety and refusal ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , personality traits ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and contrastive behavior control ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Zou et al. (2025) proposed representation engineering as a general framework for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in LLMs. The theoretical basis for these methods rests on the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ; Burns et al., 2024 ) , which posits that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in residual stream space. For reasoning specifically, SEAL ( Chen et al., 2025b ) introduced a lightweight approach to calibrating reasoning behaviors via hidden-state contrasts extracted from chain-of-thought traces, and Sinii et al. (2026) provided a mechanistic analysis of how steering vectors modify reasoning. Venhoff et al. (2025) systematically mapped steering directions to distinct reasoning behaviors. Our work builds directly on SEAL’s pipeline but addresses a fundamental limitation: the assumption that keyword-detected boundaries all encode genuine behavioral signals. Stochastic behaviors and robustness. Our work is grounded in the observation that intrinsic reasoning behaviors are stochastic rather than deterministic. Dies et al. (2026) showed that LLM belief representations can be unstable under semantic perturbations, and Wang et al. (2022) noted that behavioral features in language models vary across sampling conditions. Perez et al. (2022) demonstrated that model-written evaluations can reveal inconsistent behaviors that are not apparent from single-sample analysis. Our stability probing methodology is related to consistency-based filtering in data curation ( Swayamdipta et al., 2020 ) , where training examples are classified by their learning dynamics. We apply an analogous principle to steering vector construction: only boundaries where the model stochastically reproduces the target behavior with high probability should contribute to the steering direction. 3 Method Figure 2 : Overview of our method. Left : SEAL mixes all keyword-detected boundaries, including unstable ones that dilute the signal. Middle : Our content-aware extraction computes per-question steering directions and projects out question-specific information via SVD. Right : Stability probing re-generates from each boundary’s prefix and retains only those that reliably reproduce the target behavior. Figure 2 gives an overview of our approach. We start from the SEAL pipeline (§ 3.1 ), identify why it underperforms through a probabilistic lens (§ 3.2 ), and propose two fixes: stability filtering (§ 3.3 ) and content projection (§ 3.4 ). 3.1 Preliminaries: SEAL Steering Vectors Given a reasoning LLM and a problem set 𝒬 = { q 1 , … , q N } \mathcal{Q}=\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}\} , SEAL ( Chen et al., 2025b ) constructs a steering vector as follows. For each problem q k q_{k} , the model generates a chain-of-thought response, which is segmented into paragraphs. Each paragraph is classified as a behavior boundary or an execution segment based on the presence of reasoning-related keywords (e.g., “wait,” “verify,” “alternatively”), yielding boundary positions B k B_{k} and execution positions E k E_{k} . All hidden states below are extracted at the first token of each paragraph at a target layer ℓ \ell ; we write 𝐡 b ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{h}_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and suppress the layer index for clarity. A per-example steering vector is computed as: 𝐝 k = 1 | B k | ​ ∑ b ∈ B k 𝐡 b − 1 | E k | ​ ∑ e ∈ E k 𝐡 e , \mathbf{d}_{k}=\frac{1}{|B_{k}|}\sum_{b\in B_{k}}\mathbf{h}_{b}-\frac{1}{|E_{k}|}\sum_{e\in E_{k}}\mathbf{h}_{e}, (1) where the first term averages over behavior boundary hidden states and the second over execution hidden states. Appendix C Probe Methodology Details Behavior probe (R+T vs. E). We train a logistic regression classifier ( LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=1.0, solver=‘lbfgs’) ) to distinguish behavior boundary (R+T) hidden states from execution (E) hidden states at layer 20. We partition the 541 R+T boundaries into 5 equal stability bins of width 0.2 on [ 0 , 1 ) [0,1) and sample 22 boundaries per bin, yielding 110 R+T samples total. We then downsample E to 110 samples, giving a balanced dataset of 220 total samples spanning 88 unique questions. The 100 questions span 7 MATH subjects; we use StratifiedKFold ( n = 5 n{=}5 ) by subject label.
